library(metafor)

dat <- data.frame(
  study = c("Aronson 1948", "Ferguson & Simes 1949", "Rosenthal et al 1960", "Hart & Sutherland 1977", "Zero trial"),
  ai = c(4, 6, 3, 62, 0),
  n1i = c(123, 306, 231, 13598, 50),
  ci = c(11, 29, 11, 248, 0),
  n2i = c(139, 303, 220, 12867, 50),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

fit <- rma.mh(measure = "OR", ai = ai, n1i = n1i, ci = ci, n2i = n2i, slab = study, level = 95.0, data = dat)
print(fit)

# back on the ratio scale
pred <- predict(fit, transf = exp)
print(pred)

# funnel plot: the 95% region is centred on the common-effect estimate (decision 0020)
funnel(fit, level = 95)

funnel.caption: Each point is a study: its estimate across, its standard error down, so larger studies are at the top. The triangle is where 95% of studies would fall around the common-effect estimate if there were no bias and no heterogeneity. Asymmetry does not by itself show non-reporting bias (such as publication bias): differences between studies, bias in smaller studies and chance can all cause it. For odds ratios, the estimate and its standard error are related, which can make a funnel look asymmetric by itself. With fewer than 10 studies, tests for asymmetry are not recommended; none is run here.

interpretation.text: Assuming one effect shared by all 4 studies, the odds in the treatment groups were 0.23 times the odds in the control groups (95% CI 0.18 to 0.30). Odds are not risks, so this is not a risk ratio; the two differ most when the event is common.
